items.title: L11: Seeing the Big Picture at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At HEO level, Seeing the Big Picture usually means understanding how your area contributes to departmental and government priorities, and using that understanding to shape what your team does. At EO level the picture is often your own team's objectives; at HEO it extends to other teams, partners, customers and the political and financial context. Typical HEO evidence includes keeping up with policy changes and working out what they mean for your team's work, explaining to staff why a priority matters, and adjusting plans when the context moves. It also includes spotting links between pieces of work that other people treat separately, for example noticing that two teams are collecting the same data from the same customers. A strong example names the wider goal, says what you noticed, shows how you acted on it and gives the result. A weak example only states that you 'understand the wider picture' or lists the department's objectives without showing a decision they changed. Another weakness is describing awareness without action: reading the business plan is not evidence, but reshaping a team's workload because the business plan changed is. Assessors also look for consideration of the people affected, including customers and the public, and for sense of the costs and risks of different options. At HEO you are not expected to set departmental strategy; you are expected to connect your team's work to it, and to make choices that visibly reflect that connection. If your example stays inside a single desk or a single task, it is probably pitched below HEO.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Seeing the Big Picture at HEO level?

options.text: Reorganising team priorities after a policy change, explaining the reasons to staff and partners
Learning the department's published objectives and quoting them in team meetings and in your own annual objectives
Completing every task on the team plan to a high standard and on time
Reading the minister's speech and forwarding it to the whole team

questions.hint: Describes action driven by wider context, not only awareness.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes HEO from EO in Seeing the Big Picture?

options.text: The picture reaches other teams, partners and external context, not only your own team's objectives
The candidate must write the departmental strategy and brief ministers on it in person each month
The candidate must use more technical vocabulary about government finance
The candidate must have line-managed staff for at least a year

questions.hint: The scope of the picture widens beyond the immediate team.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes: 'I always keep the department's objectives in mind.' What is the main weakness?

options.text: It states an attitude without showing any decision the objectives changed
It is too short to be read properly at the sift stage and uses no figures at all
It refers to objectives that are not specific to the candidate's role
It credits the department instead of the individual candidate

questions.hint: Assessors need action and result, not a declared mindset.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest sign that an example is below HEO for this Behaviour?

options.text: The example involved a short deadline, some pressure and a series of small requests from colleagues
The whole story stays inside one desk or one task with no link to wider aims
The result was described in general terms rather than a figure
The candidate worked with only two other colleagues

questions.hint: HEO needs a link beyond your own task.

questions.prompt: Noticing that two teams collect the same data from the same customers is useful evidence mainly because it shows what?

options.text: You were able to complete a larger volume of data entry than your colleagues in the same period
You spotted a connection others treated separately and acted on it
You understand the technical systems used by both teams
You were able to report another team's mistakes to a manager

questions.hint: Connecting separate pieces of work is a typical HEO big-picture move.

questions.prompt: After a policy change, a HEO adjusts the team's workload. What else would strengthen the example most?

options.text: Showing how the effects on customers and partners were weighed before choosing
Adding a list of the policy's legal references and the dates on which each change took effect
Stating that the change was welcomed by all staff in the team
Explaining that the decision was made quickly to save time

questions.hint: Big Picture includes thinking about people affected and risks.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HEO expectations is the most accurate general pattern?

options.text: You set the strategy for the whole department on behalf of the senior team and report to ministers
You are expected only to follow the plan set by your line manager
You connect your team's work to departmental direction and make choices that reflect it
You are assessed on knowledge of other departments' internal budgets

questions.hint: HEOs connect rather than set strategy.

questions.prompt: A candidate reads the business plan and summarises it for the team but changes nothing. How should an assessor see this evidence?

options.text: As awareness only, because no decision or action followed from it
As strong evidence, because the summary shows understanding of the plan and informs the whole team
As leadership evidence, because information was shared with staff
As a Delivering at Pace example, because it was done on time

questions.hint: Awareness without action is weak evidence.

questions.prompt: Which result would make a Big Picture example more convincing?

options.text: A comment from the candidate that the team felt better informed and more engaged afterwards than before
An outcome linked to the wider aim, such as fewer duplicate customer requests across two teams
A note that the plan was submitted before the deadline
A statement that the example took place over several months

questions.hint: Results should tie back to the wider goal.

questions.prompt: When explaining to staff why a priority matters, what is the candidate demonstrating?

options.text: Following instructions from a more senior manager without question and passing them on unchanged
Communicating information that was already known to everyone
Avoiding discussion of risk to protect morale
Linking the wider context to the team's work so people understand the reason for choices

questions.hint: Explaining the 'why' shows context shaping team action.

items.title: L11: Changing and Improving at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Changing and Improving at HEO level typically asks you to seek out and lead improvement, not only suggest it. At EO level a good example might be a new routine adopted by a small team. At HEO level assessors usually look for a change that crosses a process, a team or a customer journey, with evidence of how the need was identified, how the change was designed and tested, how people were brought with you, and what difference it made. A common structure is: a problem measured with data, options considered, a pilot, a decision, implementation, a review and a result. Good evidence often shows that the candidate dealt with resistance, for example by listening to concerns and altering the plan, and that the change was checked against its intended benefit rather than assumed to work. Changing also includes responding to change imposed from outside, such as a new system or policy, by helping a team adapt. Risks matter: HEO answers should show the candidate thought about what could go wrong and put in place something to manage it, such as a pilot or a fallback. Weak examples include suggesting an idea that someone else then built, improving a personal habit, or describing a change with no evidence it worked. Another weakness is a change that only the candidate's manager led while the candidate administered it. Remember to separate what you did from what the project did, and say how you measured the improvement, for instance a reduction in processing time, error rate or complaints, in general terms if figures are sensitive.

questions.prompt: Which example best matches Changing and Improving at HEO level?

options.text: Suggesting a better filing layout for the shared drive that a colleague then introduced across the whole team
Leading a pilot of a redesigned process across two teams, adjusting it after feedback and measuring the benefit
Keeping a personal checklist that reduced your own errors
Attending a workshop on process improvement and sharing the slides

questions.hint: Leading, testing and measuring a change that crosses a process.

questions.prompt: Why is a pilot useful evidence in a HEO improvement example?

options.text: It shows the candidate avoided making a firm decision about the change until others had approved it
It shows the change was too small to need approval
It shows the candidate was following a template given by the department
It shows risk was managed and the change was tested before full rollout

questions.hint: Testing before rolling out shows thought about risk.

questions.prompt: A candidate says the new process 'worked well' without further detail. What is the problem?

options.text: The candidate did not mention that the work was done in a team
The word 'process' suggests the work was too administrative
There is no measure or comparison showing that the benefit was real
The example is too long for the word count

questions.hint: Improvements should be checked against an intended benefit.

questions.prompt: Which description is most clearly too junior for HEO?

options.text: Chairing a review of how a recent change had affected customer complaints and team workloads
Redesigning a form after analysing why it produced errors
Suggesting an idea to the manager, who built and ran the improvement
Running a trial of a new step in a shared process

questions.hint: Passing on an idea without leading anything is below HEO.

questions.prompt: When colleagues resist a change, which candidate action would assessors usually value most?

options.text: Listening to their concerns and adapting the plan where the concerns were sound
Insisting on the original plan to show determination and avoid reopening the decision
Asking the manager to tell the team to comply
Leaving out the resisting staff to avoid delay

questions.hint: Bringing people with you is part of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: What does the Behaviour mean when it includes responding to imposed change?

options.text: Accepting every change without raising any questions about it so as not to slow the work down
Reversing changes that were decided by the department
Helping a team adapt to a new system or policy, not only starting your own ideas
Waiting for guidance before taking any action on the change

questions.hint: Adapting to change is also evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is the typical structure of a strong HEO improvement story?

options.text: Idea, immediate rollout to all teams, an announcement and a note of thanks to those involved
Instruction from manager, task completion, thanks from team
Complaint, apology, return to the old way of working
Measured problem, options, trial, decision, implementation, review of the result

questions.hint: Evidence of design, testing and review distinguishes HEO answers.

questions.prompt: A candidate led a change but the plan came entirely from the project board. What should they do in the statement?

options.text: Describe the whole project as their own work in order to show the full scope of the change
Leave out the project and describe only a smaller task
Name the project board members and their responsibilities
Separate what they personally did from what the project as a whole did

questions.hint: Attribution of your own contribution is essential.

questions.prompt: Which measure is most appropriate as the result of a process improvement?

options.text: The number of meetings and workshops held while the change was being designed and agreed
The length of the project plan produced
The number of staff who attended the launch briefing
A reduction in processing time or error rate compared with before the change

questions.hint: A before-and-after measure shows the improvement.

questions.prompt: Which risk step would strengthen a HEO answer?

options.text: Identifying what could go wrong and arranging a fallback before launch
Describing the expected benefits in the strongest possible language so that sponsors back the launch
Arguing that risk is the responsibility of senior leaders
Leaving risks to be found by users after launch

questions.hint: HEO answers show thought about risk.

items.title: L11: Making Effective Decisions at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At HEO level, Making Effective Decisions usually involves decisions that affect others, made with incomplete or conflicting information and in the face of competing interests. Assessors commonly look for a sequence: you gathered and checked relevant information, consulted the right people, considered options and risks, made a timely decision, explained it, and took responsibility for the outcome, including reviewing it afterwards. Two features separate HEO from EO. The first is scope: the decision has consequences for other people or for other teams. The second is judgement under uncertainty: there was no obviously right answer, and you could not wait for perfect information. Typical HEO examples are choosing which of several competing requests to prioritise, deciding whether to escalate an issue or deal with it locally, or deciding how to allocate limited resources between teams. Strong answers say what the options were and why you ruled some out, not only what you chose. Using data and advice matters, but a decision that is only 'I asked my manager and did what they said' is usually too junior. Equally, deciding without consulting people who were affected can look reckless. Honesty also matters: Civil Service values require objectivity, so a good example does not conceal risks or ignore evidence that points the other way. You should also show that you owned the outcome. If it went partly wrong, say what you did to put it right and what you learned. HEO decisions are rarely perfect, and assessors know it.

questions.prompt: What two features usually separate a HEO decision example from an EO one?

options.text: A longer written description and more technical vocabulary
A formal approval from a minister and a legal opinion on the decision taken
Wider consequences for others and judgement under uncertainty
A larger team and a longer time frame for the work

questions.hint: Scope and uncertainty are the typical HEO markers.

questions.prompt: Which decision would usually be too junior to evidence this Behaviour at HEO?

options.text: Asking the manager what to do and carrying out the instruction
Choosing between competing requests from two teams with different deadlines
Deciding whether an issue needed escalating or local action
Allocating a limited budget between workstreams

questions.hint: Taking instructions is not decision-making.

questions.prompt: Why should a strong answer describe the options ruled out?

options.text: It allows the candidate to write more words for the same effort without adding new material
It shows the reasoning behind the choice and not only the result
It proves that the final decision was correct
It shows that a manager approved each option

questions.hint: Reasoning is what assessors are scoring.

questions.prompt: A candidate decided without consulting people who would be affected. What is the main risk to the evidence?

options.text: It will always be marked as too senior for the role and returned to the candidate unscored
It suggests the candidate used too much data
It shows that the decision was made too slowly
It can look reckless and show a gap in Working Together as well

questions.hint: Consultation of affected people is part of an effective decision.

questions.prompt: Which element reflects the Civil Service value of objectivity in a decision answer?

options.text: Choosing the option that was quickest to explain to the senior manager and the wider team
Giving the option the senior manager favoured
Selecting whichever option had the lowest cost
Weighing evidence that pointed against your preferred option

questions.hint: Objectivity means considering evidence fairly.

questions.prompt: A decision partly failed. What would assessors value most in the candidate's answer?

options.text: Explaining that the information given by colleagues was incomplete and out of date at the time
Owning the outcome, putting it right and saying what was learned
Showing that others made the same error
Leaving out the failure and focusing on the successful parts

questions.hint: Accountability and learning matter at HEO.

questions.prompt: Which situation best shows decision-making under incomplete information?

options.text: Choosing how to respond to a surge in demand before the cause was confirmed
Following a documented procedure for a routine request
Updating a spreadsheet using figures supplied by a colleague and checking the formulas against last month
Selecting a date for a meeting from three offered by the attendees

questions.hint: No obvious right answer and no time for full data.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate describe data and advice used in a decision?

options.text: Say what was gathered and how it influenced the options and the choice
List every source consulted in date order without explaining how each one was used in the choice
State that the data confirmed the decision already made
Avoid naming sources to protect confidentiality in all cases

questions.hint: Show the link between information and choice.

questions.prompt: Which closing step helps show effective decision-making?

options.text: Passing the decision record to the archive and informing the corporate governance team
Reviewing the outcome afterwards against what was expected
Thanking everyone who attended the discussions
Waiting to see whether anyone complained

questions.hint: Review shows ownership beyond the moment of decision.

questions.prompt: A candidate says: 'I decided quickly because the deadline was close.' What detail is missing from this example?

options.text: The names of every colleague who was in the room and the order in which they spoke
The date and time of the deadline in the team's diary
A statement that other people were happy with the outcome
The options, risks and reasons that show how the decision was reached

questions.hint: Speed alone is not reasoning.

items.title: L11: Leadership at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Leadership at HEO is often misunderstood as line management. The Success Profiles Behaviour is about how you lead, not whether you have a title. At HEO level assessors typically expect you to set a clear direction for a team or a piece of work, motivate people through pressure or change, give them the context they need, challenge poor practice and take responsibility for the outcome. Examples often include leading a team through a reorganisation, leading a project without formal authority over the people in it, or setting the tone after a setback. Good evidence shows what you said and did, how people responded and what resulted. A HEO who describes 'managing a team of six' without saying what direction was set or what challenges were met has described a post, not leadership. Likewise, leading by instruction alone, with no effort to explain or involve people, is a weak example. Leadership also includes inclusion: noticing who is not being heard and making sure they are, and behaving in line with the Civil Service Code, for example by being honest about difficult news. Where you led by influence, such as chairing a working group of peers, say how you gained support. For people who do not line-manage, examples such as leading a project, coordinating an event or running a rota are acceptable if the scope is real. Avoid claiming credit for team success without describing your own part, and avoid describing leadership as always being present and busy; assessors look for effect.

questions.prompt: Which description best reflects how assessors view leadership at HEO?

options.text: The size of the team shown on your organisation chart and the grades of those reporting to you
The number of years spent in a supervisory post
Whether your name appears on the approval of expenses
How you set direction, motivate others and take responsibility, with or without a formal title

questions.hint: Leadership is about behaviour, not job title.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes: 'I manage a team of six.' What is missing?

options.text: The names and grades of the six staff and the date on which each of them joined
A statement of the team's annual budget
What direction was set and what leadership challenge was handled
A reference to the department's management training

questions.hint: A post is not evidence until behaviour is described.

questions.prompt: Which example would suit a HEO candidate with no line reports?

options.text: Leading a cross-team working group and securing agreement through influence
Describing the daily tasks of a post in detail, without any people responsibility to mention
Taking part in a group that another person chaired
Attending leadership training in the department

questions.hint: Leading by influence is acceptable if scope is real.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows challenging poor practice at HEO level?

options.text: Reporting the colleague to the manager first, without speaking to them about the shortcut in person
Ignoring the shortcut because the target was met
Raising a colleague's shortcut with them, agreeing the correct method and following it up
Rewriting the process without telling anybody

questions.hint: Constructive, direct challenge shows leadership.

questions.prompt: Why is leading by instruction alone a weaker example?

options.text: It always breaches the Civil Service Code because it removes people's right to be consulted
It shows the candidate lacks technical knowledge
It gives no sign of explaining, motivating or involving the people affected
It produces slow results in every situation

questions.hint: Leadership includes bringing people with you.

questions.prompt: What does the inclusion element of Leadership usually involve?

options.text: Ensuring every person in the team has the same working pattern and the same development plan
Choosing team members who share the leader's approach
Limiting meetings to those directly responsible for a task
Noticing who is not being heard and making sure their views are included

questions.hint: Inclusive leadership gives all voices a hearing.

questions.prompt: During a reorganisation, which statement shows leadership rather than management?

options.text: I distributed the new structure chart, allocated desks and updated the contact list for the whole department
I made sure the usual weekly reports were still completed
I forwarded the human resources guidance to all staff
I explained why the changes were happening, acknowledged concerns and agreed how we would work through them

questions.hint: Direction, context and motivation define leadership.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate handle credit for team success in a Leadership answer?

options.text: Present the whole team's achievement as personal
Avoid mentioning the result altogether so as not to be seen to overclaim on the team's behalf
Describe their own actions and what changed because of them
Credit the manager for every positive outcome

questions.hint: Own contribution must be clear.

questions.prompt: Which point about difficult news fits the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Delaying the news until after a busy period so that the team can finish its current deliverables
Sharing only the positive parts to protect morale
Being honest and clear with the team while explaining what support is available
Letting the team hear it from other sources

questions.hint: Honesty is a core value in leadership.

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of describing leadership as 'always being present and busy'?

options.text: It shows that the candidate works too many hours and is not delegating to the rest of the team
It describes effort and not the effect on people or results
It means the candidate is not delegating tasks
It suggests the team has too few staff

questions.hint: Assessors look for effect.

items.title: L11: Communicating and Influencing at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At HEO level, Communicating and Influencing usually involves persuading people over whom you have no direct authority, handling difficult or sensitive messages, and adapting your message for different audiences. Typical evidence includes presenting a case to senior colleagues, negotiating between teams, writing a briefing for a decision-maker, or explaining a technical subject to the public. Assessors usually expect you to show that you understood the audience before choosing the message, that you chose a suitable format, and that you checked that the message was understood. Influence is shown by a change in what someone did or decided, so the result should be stated: a plan was agreed, a request approved or a problem prevented. Good answers also include handling disagreement, such as responding to challenge calmly and with evidence, without damaging the relationship. Strong HEO answers distinguish between informing and influencing. A newsletter to staff is communication; persuading a reluctant partner to share data is influence. Plain English matters at every grade, and so does honesty: influence by exaggeration or by withholding material facts is inconsistent with the Civil Service Code. Weak examples include a long list of meetings attended, a description of a routine email or a presentation with no information about the audience or the result. Where the influence was exerted in writing, such as a submission to a minister's office, say what you wrote and what you wanted the reader to do. If a colleague helped draft the message, say what you contributed. Keep the example specific, and use direct reported effect.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes influencing from simply informing?

options.text: Influencing changes what someone decides or does, while informing passes on facts
Influencing uses longer documents than informing and is aimed at larger numbers of people
Influencing is always done in person while informing is written
Influencing happens only with senior staff

questions.hint: Influence is shown by effect.

questions.prompt: A candidate lists the meetings they attended and presentations they gave. What is the weakness?

options.text: The list is too long to fit inside the word limit of a written statement at sift
There is no audience analysis, message choice or result
It describes work carried out with senior colleagues
It shows communication in a face-to-face setting only

questions.hint: Activity is not evidence of influence.

questions.prompt: Which of these best shows influence at HEO level?

options.text: Persuading a reluctant partner team to share data, by addressing their concerns with evidence
Sending the whole department a monthly newsletter
Writing the minutes of the quarterly partner meeting that were approved without amendment
Presenting figures on a slide deck prepared by another team

questions.hint: Persuading without authority is typical HEO evidence.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate show about the audience in a strong answer?

options.text: That they understood the audience's needs and concerns before shaping the message
That the audience was senior to them in grade and unfamiliar with the subject at hand
That the audience attended every briefing arranged
That the audience was larger than ten people

questions.hint: Audience understanding drives message design.

questions.prompt: During a challenge to your proposal, which response best reflects the Behaviour?

options.text: Withdrawing the proposal to avoid conflict and offering to bring a revised one later
Repeating the same argument more forcefully
Responding calmly with evidence and keeping the relationship intact
Asking your manager to answer on your behalf

questions.hint: Handling challenge calmly and with evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is influence by exaggeration a problem in a Civil Service example?

options.text: It is unlikely to persuade experienced colleagues
It requires more preparation than a straightforward case and is harder to defend at interview
It conflicts with the Civil Service Code values of honesty and objectivity
It only works with external audiences

questions.hint: Honesty and objectivity apply to influence too.

questions.prompt: Which submission example is strongest?

options.text: I wrote a long briefing covering every piece of background so the decision-maker had full information, and it was acknowledged by their office
I wrote a one-page briefing setting out three options and asked the decision-maker to choose by Friday, and the preferred option was agreed
I drafted a submission for my manager to sign
I proofread a briefing prepared by a colleague

questions.hint: Clear ask, clear reader, stated result.

questions.prompt: How can a candidate show that a message was understood?

options.text: By noting that the message was sent on time
By counting how many people received it
By checking back with the audience, for example through questions or follow-up actions
By assuming that silence from the audience meant agreement and moving on to the next item

questions.hint: Check understanding rather than assuming it.

questions.prompt: If a colleague helped draft the message, what should the candidate do in the statement?

options.text: Say what they personally contributed to the content and delivery
Leave out the colleague's help altogether so that the statement reads as a single clear story
Credit the colleague with the whole piece
Describe only the colleague's contribution

questions.hint: Own contribution must be clear.

questions.prompt: Which format choice shows good judgement for explaining a technical topic to the public?

options.text: A dense technical annex with all of the terminology and references for those who want detail
Plain English with a short example and a chance to ask questions
A shortened version of the internal policy paper
A verbal summary with no written follow-up

questions.hint: Plain English matches the audience.

items.title: L11: Working Together at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At HEO level, Working Together usually means building and maintaining relationships across boundaries, and managing the tensions that arise when different parties have competing priorities. Typical evidence includes working with another team or department on shared delivery, bringing external partners into a project, resolving a conflict between people or groups, and making sure that your own team's interests do not overshadow wider goals. A common distinction with EO level is that EO evidence is about co-operating well with colleagues, while HEO evidence is about building collaboration actively and handling disagreement between others. Good answers say who the parties were, what they wanted, where they disagreed, what the candidate did and what the result was for the shared goal and the relationship. It is useful to show that you looked for common ground, were open about your own constraints, and respected views that differed from your own. Diversity and inclusion are part of the Behaviour, so examples about drawing in people from different backgrounds or working patterns, or adjusting a process so that part-time or remote colleagues can contribute fully, are relevant. Be careful not to confuse Working Together with Communicating and Influencing: if the central point is persuading someone, that may belong with the latter, whereas if it is building a joint way of working and sharing credit, it belongs with Working Together. Weak examples describe being friendly, helping one colleague with a task, or working in a team that happened to be co-located. Always make clear what you personally did to build the collaboration.

questions.prompt: What usually separates HEO from EO evidence in Working Together?

options.text: Building collaboration across boundaries and handling disagreement between others
Working with a larger number of colleagues in the same office and attending more team meetings
Using more formal meetings to coordinate tasks
Working only with senior colleagues

questions.hint: HEO builds and manages collaboration actively.

questions.prompt: Which example is the strongest HEO evidence for this Behaviour?

options.text: Helping a colleague in another team to complete a late task and then checking they had what they needed to finish the rest of it
Attending a team meeting each week
Being friendly with colleagues in other departments
Resolving a disagreement between two partner teams over shared data by finding common ground and sharing credit

questions.hint: Brokering collaboration across parties is typical HEO.

questions.prompt: A candidate's example is mainly about persuading a reluctant manager to accept a plan. Which Behaviour does it probably fit better?

options.text: Working Together
Managing a Quality Service
Communicating and Influencing
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: Persuasion is the central action.

questions.prompt: Which element of the example signals the diversity and inclusion part of the Behaviour?

options.text: Adjusting meeting arrangements so remote and part-time colleagues could contribute fully
Choosing the team members who were available on all days of the week to take on the project work
Keeping meetings to a fixed length
Using standard templates for all agendas

questions.hint: Inclusive practice is part of Working Together.

questions.prompt: What should the answer show about the parties involved?

options.text: Who they were, what each wanted and where they disagreed
Their job titles, grades and years of service in the Civil Service
Their opinions of the candidate
Their relationships with the candidate's manager

questions.hint: Understanding competing interests is essential.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows respect for views that differ from your own?

options.text: Explaining your own position again with more detail so that the other team can see its merits
Agreeing quickly to avoid delay
Asking for the reasons behind the other team's position and adapting the plan where justified
Recording their objection and proceeding

questions.hint: Seeking to understand shows respect.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I get on well with everyone' weak evidence?

options.text: It is too informal for a written statement and does not match the wording of the advert
It contradicts the idea of challenge
It suggests the candidate avoids conflict
It describes a personal trait without any action, context or result

questions.hint: Evidence is behaviour with outcome.

questions.prompt: How does being open about your own constraints help collaboration?

options.text: It prevents the others from asking you for further help once the work has been agreed
It allows you to avoid responsibility for the result
It builds trust and helps others plan realistic joint arrangements
It gives the other party a reason to escalate

questions.hint: Transparency builds trust.

questions.prompt: A HEO example where the candidate's team gained everything and the partner team lost out has what weakness?

options.text: It shows the candidate worked too hard for the team and neglected colleagues elsewhere in the department
It has too many parties involved
It was not recorded in a formal agreement
The team's interests overshadowed the shared goal and the partner relationship

questions.hint: HEO collaboration serves wider goals.

questions.prompt: Which result most strongly completes a Working Together example?

options.text: The meeting finished on time
The partners agreed to meet again some time later in the year to review the arrangements
The candidate received positive comments from a manager
The shared goal was delivered and the relationship was stronger afterwards

questions.hint: Results cover both goal and relationship.

items.title: L11: Developing Self and Others at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Developing Self and Others at HEO level has two halves, and strong answers usually cover both. Developing yourself means identifying your own gaps honestly, planning how to close them and applying what you have learned; seeking feedback and acting on it counts as much as formal courses. Developing others at HEO usually includes setting clear objectives, giving regular and honest feedback, coaching, delegating in a way that stretches people, handling a performance concern fairly and supporting someone's career. A HEO who simply sends staff on training has shown little. Assessors look for how you identified the person's need, what you did that was tailored to them, how you checked progress, and what changed. Good examples include taking a struggling team member from missed deadlines to consistent delivery through clear expectations and regular check-ins, or coaching a new manager. Because staff matters are confidential, describe the situation in general terms and focus on your actions rather than private circumstances. Feedback must be specific, timely and balanced; a vague comment that someone 'needs to try harder' is not developmental. Development can also be informal, such as pairing a junior colleague with an experienced one or giving a stretching task with support. If you do not line-manage, consider mentoring, buddying or leading a learning session. A weakness is writing only about your own courses, or describing a training programme you merely administered. Another is claiming the success of someone you developed without saying what you actually did. Self-development evidence should include something you changed in your own practice as a result of feedback.

questions.prompt: Which pairing summarises the two halves of this Behaviour?

options.text: Attending courses and recording attendance
Developing yourself honestly and developing other people in a tailored way
Giving feedback and receiving feedback in annual reviews
Following your own career plan carefully and advising other people on their career plans

questions.hint: Strong answers usually cover both self and others.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest example of developing others at HEO?

options.text: Setting clear objectives with a team member who was missing deadlines, checking in regularly and seeing their delivery improve
Booking a team member onto a course that was recommended by the learning team, then recording their attendance and the course feedback score
Sharing the department's learning catalogue with the team
Telling a team member that they needed to try harder

questions.hint: Tailored, tracked support with a result.

questions.prompt: Why is sending staff on training alone weak evidence?

options.text: It shows that the candidate has no budget
It shows no identification of need, tailoring or follow-up
It suggests that the staff did not want to attend and were sent against their wishes
It implies the training was not approved

questions.hint: The candidate's own actions must be visible.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate describe a performance concern in a statement?

options.text: With the staff member's full name and circumstances
Only after the matter is closed, the records are deleted and the person has left the team
By not mentioning that there was a performance concern
In general terms, focusing on their own actions and avoiding private details

questions.hint: Confidentiality matters while still showing action.

questions.prompt: Which feedback example is most developmental?

options.text: Telling someone that they need to be better at writing and giving them a list of books on the subject
Praising someone publicly for working hard
Leaving feedback to the annual review
Telling someone that the first half of a report was clear and showing how to tighten the conclusion

questions.hint: Specific, timely and balanced feedback helps.

questions.prompt: What can a HEO without line reports offer as developing-others evidence?

options.text: A summary of the department's training policy and the budget available for learning each year
A description of the candidate's own course
Mentoring, buddying a new starter or leading a learning session
A list of colleagues who report to their manager

questions.hint: Development does not require line management.

questions.prompt: What should be included in a self-development example?

options.text: A list of courses with their dates
A statement that you enjoy learning new things and always take up courses when offered
Something changed in your practice after feedback or learning
A note of how many hours were spent on training

questions.hint: Applying learning shows development.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'my team member was promoted' with no description of their own actions. What is the issue?

options.text: The candidate should not mention a promotion in a statement because it is private to the person
The candidate claims the outcome without showing their contribution to it
The example is too recent to be believable
Promotion cannot be evidence for a Behaviour

questions.hint: Own actions need to be evident.

questions.prompt: What does delegating in a way that stretches people involve?

options.text: Giving a task a little beyond their experience with support and clear expectations
Giving the task with no guidance and no check-ins, to see how they cope on their own
Assigning only tasks the person has done before
Passing on unwelcome tasks to free your own time

questions.hint: Stretch with support develops people.

questions.prompt: Which step shows you checked progress in developing someone?

options.text: Agreeing review points and comparing their work with the objectives set
Asking a colleague whether the person seemed happier and more settled in the team lately
Waiting for the person to raise any problems
Looking at their attendance record only

questions.hint: Monitoring against objectives shows follow-through.

items.title: L11: Managing a Quality Service at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Managing a Quality Service at HEO level generally asks you to take responsibility for the standard of a service, not only to follow it. Typical HEO evidence includes setting and monitoring standards, using management information to spot problems, balancing quality against cost and speed, managing risk, handling complaints and making sure customers' needs are central. The EO pattern is checking work, tracking errors and acting on patterns for a small team; the HEO pattern extends this to a service or process involving several people or teams, with decisions about resources and priorities. A strong answer states the standard, how it was measured, what the data showed, what action you took, and what changed for customers or users. Examples include redesigning a quality-assurance process after finding that errors clustered at one step, negotiating a service standard with a partner team, or establishing a feedback loop with customers. Public service also means fairness and accessibility, so consider whether the service works for people with different needs. Compliance is part of quality: following legal and policy requirements, such as data protection, and keeping accurate records are expected. Weak examples describe working carefully, checking your own work only or reacting to individual complaints without looking for patterns. Another weakness is stating that quality was good without naming a standard or measure. Be careful with confidential data: describe the type of measure, such as a percentage of cases completed within a target time, in general terms where figures are sensitive. Always say what you personally decided or changed.

questions.prompt: What generally separates HEO from EO in Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Using a longer checklist for the same tasks and signing off a larger number of cases personally
Responsibility for the standard of a wider service involving several people or teams
Working to stricter deadlines
Dealing only with complex individual complaints

questions.hint: HEO extends to service-level responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best structures a HEO quality answer?

options.text: Task, deadline, completion, manager's thanks and then closure of the case file
Standard, measure, data findings, action, customer result
Complaint, apology, refund, close
Instruction, checking, sign-off, close

questions.hint: Standards and data lead to action.

questions.prompt: A candidate finds errors cluster at one step in a process. Which HEO action would be strongest?

options.text: Ask staff at that step to be more careful and remind them of the quality standard in writing
Report the clustering to a manager and wait
Redesign the quality checks at that step and measure the effect on errors
Correct each error individually when it is found

questions.hint: Systematic action addresses the cause.

questions.prompt: Why is handling complaints one at a time weaker evidence than finding patterns?

options.text: Individual complaints are not part of the service and are dealt with by a separate team elsewhere
Pattern analysis is faster than individual replies
Managers prefer fewer complaints to be recorded
Patterns point to causes that can be fixed for all customers

questions.hint: Look for systemic improvement.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows quality balanced against cost and speed?

options.text: I weighed adding a second check against the delay it would cause and trialled it on the highest-risk cases first
I applied every possible check to all cases whatever the cost or the delay it caused customers
I removed checks to meet the deadline
I left the checks to the next team in the process

questions.hint: Balancing priorities shows HEO judgement.

questions.prompt: Why does accessibility matter in a quality example?

options.text: It reduces the cost of printing and posting paper forms to customers each year
A quality public service must work fairly for people with different needs
It is required only for services used by the public online
It applies only to HR processes

questions.hint: Fairness is part of public service quality.

questions.prompt: Which is the weakest way to describe quality evidence?

options.text: 'Cases completed within target rose after I changed the second check.'
'Quality of the service was good under my management.'
'Customer survey scores rose after the new form was introduced.'
'Errors at one step fell once the process was redesigned.'

questions.hint: No standard or measure is named.

questions.prompt: How might a candidate handle sensitive figures in the answer?

options.text: Leave out the measure completely
Quote private case details to show accuracy and demonstrate that you handled live casework
Describe the type of measure in general terms, such as the share of cases within target
Round every figure to zero

questions.hint: Measures can be described without breaching confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Which part of quality is also about compliance?

options.text: Choosing the fastest option for each case
Following data protection rules and keeping accurate records
Reducing the number of staff checking the work to keep the cost of each case down
Avoiding customer contact to prevent complaints

questions.hint: Compliance underpins quality.

questions.prompt: Which action shows a feedback loop with customers?

options.text: Sending a standard thank-you letter after each case with a contact number for queries
Surveying users after a case closes and changing a step because of the results
Recording the number of customer calls each day
Asking colleagues what they thought of the service

questions.hint: Feedback must lead to a change.

items.title: L11: Delivering at Pace at HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Delivering at Pace at HEO level usually involves taking responsibility for results that depend on other people and on competing demands. Typical evidence includes planning and prioritising a team's work, managing resources and risks, keeping delivery on track when priorities change, and maintaining standards under pressure. At EO level a good example may be planning a small team's work over a week; at HEO it extends to a programme of work, several workstreams or a delivery with external dependencies. Assessors usually look for a clear goal, a plan, how you monitored progress, how you dealt with obstacles, how you maintained quality and what was achieved by when. Good answers also show that you made trade-offs: what you decided to delay or stop, and why. Delivering at pace does not mean working long hours yourself. A HEO who solved a delivery problem by personally working every evening has shown commitment but not necessarily management; showing how you reallocated work, negotiated priorities or removed blockers is stronger. Pace and quality must both appear: finishing early with errors is weak evidence. Include how you kept people informed and how you protected the wellbeing of the team under pressure, since sustainable delivery is part of the Behaviour. Weak examples are routine tasks with a fixed deadline, a project where someone else made all the key choices, or descriptions with no dates, scale or result. If dates or numbers are sensitive, use general terms such as 'two weeks ahead of schedule' or 'with a 20 per cent smaller team'. Always say what you personally controlled.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Delivering at Pace at HEO?

options.text: Delivering a multi-team piece of work to a changed deadline by reprioritising tasks and negotiating what could wait
Completing a daily batch of cases before the end of the day, staying late on busy days and clearing every item from the queue
Working late every evening to finish a report
Following a project plan produced by the project manager

questions.hint: Trade-offs and coordination show HEO scope.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with solving a delivery problem only by working long hours?

options.text: It breaks working time regulations in every case and puts the team at risk of formal action
It is likely to be impossible in a busy team
It shows personal effort but not management of people, priorities or blockers
It shows that the deadline was set too early

questions.hint: Management evidence is stronger than effort.

questions.prompt: Which element would make an answer stronger?

options.text: Listing all of the tasks on the project plan, with owners and dates against each one
Describing the number of meetings held
Saying what you decided to delay or stop and why
Stating that the team worked hard

questions.hint: Trade-offs show judgement.

questions.prompt: A candidate finished early but with errors that had to be corrected. How would this be seen?

options.text: As strong evidence, because the deadline was beaten
As good evidence of a risk-based approach
As evidence of excellent team motivation, since the work was finished so far ahead of the date
As weak evidence, because pace and quality must both appear

questions.hint: Delivery without quality is not enough.

questions.prompt: How should wellbeing appear in a HEO pace example?

options.text: By showing how the workload was shared and people were supported under pressure
By stating that nobody took leave during the period and everyone stayed to the end of the project
By describing how the staff were thanked afterwards
By avoiding any reference to difficulties

questions.hint: Sustainable delivery is part of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which feature suggests the example is too junior?

options.text: A team of five with some external dependencies and a deadline that was changed by a senior manager
A change to the plan caused by a new government priority
A routine task with a fixed deadline and no choices made by the candidate
A decision to hand over one workstream to another team

questions.hint: No judgement or ownership.

questions.prompt: How might a candidate describe sensitive dates or numbers?

options.text: By omitting any mention of the timescale and describing only the final product that was delivered
With exact internal reference codes
By quoting the figures supplied by a manager
In general terms, such as ahead of schedule or with a smaller team

questions.hint: General terms preserve confidentiality yet give scale.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows monitoring progress?

options.text: Asking staff to say if they were behind
Reviewing the outcome only after delivery and recording lessons for the next project in the file
Agreeing weekly milestones, tracking them and acting when one slipped
Leaving tracking to a project office

questions.hint: Active monitoring supports control.

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate state what they personally controlled?

options.text: Because it makes the statement longer
Because assessors need to separate individual actions from decisions made by others
Because it avoids mention of the team
Because it shows independence from managers and proves that the candidate works without supervision

questions.hint: Individual contribution must be visible.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical HEO obstacle that a strong answer would address?

options.text: A dependency on an external partner that is running late
A colleague taking a day's leave during the final week of the project, with no cover arranged
A routine request arriving from another team in the same week
A small change to the template used for the weekly report

questions.hint: External dependencies are typical at HEO.

items.title: L11: When the evidence is about the team, not you
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A frequent reason for a lower sift score is that the evidence describes what the team did rather than what the candidate did. Assessors can only score the individual, so statements built on 'we' leave them guessing. This is not a rule against the word 'we'. Teams do the work, and honest answers acknowledge it. The test is whether the reader can tell, for each key step, who did it. A useful method is to write the first draft in the first person singular for every action you personally took, and to use 'we' only for context or results that you shared. For example: 'The team had a backlog of 400 cases. I analysed the case types, proposed a triage and led two staff through it; together we cleared the backlog in six weeks.' Here the candidate's own actions are clear, and the shared result is credited honestly. The opposite error is claiming everything: 'I redesigned the service' when you contributed one stage. Overclaiming can be exposed by interview questions and by references, and it conflicts with the honesty expected under the Civil Service Code. Another variation is using a leader's decisions as your own: if your manager decided and you carried out, the evidence is about implementation, not decision-making. If your role in a team effort was small, choose a different example. Where leadership is the Behaviour, a statement such as 'the team was motivated' is weaker than naming what you said and did that motivated them and how you knew it worked. Always check that every paragraph contains at least one verb in the first person singular describing a real action.

questions.prompt: Why is evidence written wholly in 'we' a problem at the sift?

options.text: Assessors can score only the individual, and cannot tell what you personally did
The word 'we' is banned by the Civil Service Code, so any use of it is marked down
It makes the statement longer than the word limit
It suggests that the team has no manager

questions.hint: Only your own actions can be scored.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best balances individual action and shared result?

options.text: We analysed the case types, proposed a triage and led the staff through it, and as a team we cleared the whole backlog
I cleared the backlog on my own over six weeks
The backlog was cleared after a triage was introduced
I analysed the case types, proposed a triage and led two staff through it; together we cleared the backlog

questions.hint: Clear actions plus honest shared result.

questions.prompt: What is the opposite error to using 'we' throughout?

options.text: Using too many figures in the description so that the actions are hard to find
Naming the colleagues who took part
Describing the context before the actions
Claiming the whole outcome when you contributed only one stage

questions.hint: Overclaiming is equally damaging.

questions.prompt: How can overclaiming be exposed?

options.text: By the word count of the statement and the number of verbs used in each paragraph
By the use of unfamiliar vocabulary
By the order in which paragraphs appear
By follow-up questions at interview and by references

questions.hint: Honesty is tested later in the process.

questions.prompt: Your manager decided on the new process and you carried it out. Which Behaviour is that evidence least suited to?

options.text: Delivering at Pace
Making Effective Decisions
Managing a Quality Service
Working Together

questions.hint: Implementation is not decision-making.

questions.prompt: A candidate's role in a team effort was minor. What is usually the best action?

options.text: Present the team's success as their own, to show the scale of what was achieved
Choose a different example where their own part was larger
Describe the project in the third person
List every task the team carried out

questions.hint: Evidence must show your own contribution.

questions.prompt: For a Leadership example, which phrasing is stronger?

options.text: The team stayed motivated throughout the whole change, and I made sure morale was high at every single stage of it
I made sure the team stayed motivated
I explained the reason for the change to each person and adjusted workloads where they raised problems
Everyone was supportive of the change

questions.hint: Name what you said and did.

questions.prompt: What quick check can a candidate run on each paragraph?

options.text: Does it contain a first-person verb describing a real action?
Does it contain at least one figure or percentage supporting the claim being made?
Does it mention the manager by name?
Does it use words from the advert?

questions.hint: First-person actions show attribution.

questions.prompt: What is the best use of 'we' in an honest answer?

options.text: For every step of the story, to be fair to others who worked on it with you
For the actions you would prefer not to take credit for
For the result only when it is poor
For shared context or results, with your own actions stated separately

questions.hint: Use 'we' where it is accurate.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes 'The team improved customer satisfaction.' What addition would help most?

options.text: What the candidate personally did and how they know it improved things
The names and grades of the other team members who contributed to the improvement
A note that the team met regularly
A statement that the manager was pleased

questions.hint: Add action and evidence.

items.title: L11: Vague evidence and how to sharpen it
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Vague evidence is a leading cause of low sift marks. Assessors score what is on the page; they cannot give credit for what you meant. Vagueness usually takes four forms. The first is generalities, such as 'I always communicate well', which state a trait without a situation. The second is missing scale: how many people, how much money or work, how long, which customers. The third is missing action detail, such as 'I dealt with the issue' without saying how. The fourth is a missing or soft result, such as 'it went well'. To sharpen an answer, add the specific situation, the particular steps you took in order, the reasons for your choices and a measured or observed result. Figures help, but they must be true and defensible. Where exact data is not available or is sensitive, use honest approximations such as 'around a third' or a general measure such as 'within target'. Quote only what you can support at interview. Avoid jargon and unexplained acronyms, since assessors may not know your area. Equally, detail should be relevant: background that does not show the Behaviour wastes words. The STAR structure, Situation, Task, Action and Result, helps, but should be proportionate; many assessors expect most of the words to describe actions and results. A short setup of one or two sentences is usually enough. A vague example is not made stronger by longer adjectives or more confident wording. 'I successfully managed a complex project' says nothing new compared with 'I managed a project'. Replace evaluation with fact: what was complex, in what way, and how many people, and what did you do about it?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most specific?

options.text: I worked extremely hard to reduce a large backlog and I was commended by my manager for it
I successfully managed a complex backlog
I made sure the backlog was dealt with
I reduced the backlog of 300 cases to 60 in four weeks by triaging on age and complexity

questions.hint: Names scale, action and result.

questions.prompt: What does 'I always communicate well' lack?

options.text: A mention of the manager's name and a quotation of their opinion of your communication
A particular situation showing the trait in action
A reference to written communication
A statement of how many staff were involved

questions.hint: Traits are not evidence.

questions.prompt: Which is a missing scale problem?

options.text: The statement uses too many figures and so hides the actions the candidate took
The statement describes the context first
The statement uses technical terms
The statement does not say how many people, cases or how much money were involved

questions.hint: Scale shows scope.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat a figure they cannot fully verify?

options.text: Round it up to make it clearer and more memorable for the assessor reading it
Use an honest approximation they can support at interview
Omit the result altogether
Quote it as exact to sound credible

questions.hint: Defensible figures only.

questions.prompt: Which change improves 'I dealt with the issue'?

options.text: Using stronger adjectives about the issue and its seriousness for the service
Adding the date of the issue
Stating that it was an important issue
Describing what the issue was and the steps taken in order

questions.hint: Action detail is the missing piece.

questions.prompt: Why does 'I successfully managed a complex project' add little?

options.text: It is too short to count towards the word limit and so would be ignored by the assessor
It repeats the word project
It names a project without a title
It evaluates without showing what was complex or what the candidate did

questions.hint: Evaluation is not evidence.

questions.prompt: How much of a STAR answer should usually be the setup?

options.text: One or two sentences, with most words used on actions and results
About half the answer, to explain the background fully before the actions are described
None, since the situation is known to the assessor
Several paragraphs, including history of the department

questions.hint: Actions carry the score.

questions.prompt: Which result statement is the softest and least checkable?

options.text: Complaints on that step fell by about a third
Turnaround moved from ten days to six
It went well and people were pleased
The backlog was cleared two weeks early

questions.hint: No measure or observation is given.

questions.prompt: Why should unexplained acronyms be avoided?

options.text: They are forbidden in written statements and always lead to automatic rejection at the sift
They count as more than one word each
The assessor may not know your area and cannot score what they do not understand
They show that the candidate lacks plain English

questions.hint: Assessors may be outside your area.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with adding background that does not show the Behaviour?

options.text: It makes the example look too senior
It suggests that the candidate did not follow the STAR format required by the advert
It is likely to be marked as inaccurate
It uses words that could have described actions and results

questions.hint: Words are limited.

items.title: L11: Choosing between examples at HEO level
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Most candidates have more than one possible example for each Behaviour, and choosing well is a skill. At HEO level, four tests are useful. First, scope: does the example show effect beyond your own task or desk, ideally across a team, process or other teams? Second, independence: did you work out what to do, or were you told? Third, evidence of the specific Behaviour: does the example make the assessor's job easy by showing the verbs of that Behaviour, such as deciding for Making Effective Decisions or improving for Changing and Improving? Fourth, result: can you say what changed, in terms the assessor can check? An example that scores well on all four will usually beat one that is more dramatic but unclear on your part. Recency also matters, as assessors usually prefer examples from the last two or three years unless the advert allows otherwise. Avoid using the same example for every Behaviour; a single story reused with a different emphasis looks thin, and assessors may suspect there is no depth behind it. In a written application, reusing the same story for two Behaviours can be acceptable if it is a large piece of work and the actions are different, but the safer approach is separate examples. If your best example concerns a mistake, it can still be strong if you show learning. Check the grade level wording in the advert, and ask which story best matches the described scope. An example that is impressive but belongs to a different Behaviour, for instance a good decision used for Developing Self and Others, will score less than a modest example that fits.

questions.prompt: Which four tests help choose an example at HEO?

options.text: Date, length, department and the name of the manager who supervised the work
Scope, independence, specific Behaviour evidence and result
Drama, size, novelty and humour
Length of service, grade, salary and team size

questions.hint: These are the usual tests.

questions.prompt: Candidate A has a dramatic story where their own part is unclear. Candidate B has a modest story with a clear personal role and result. Which usually scores higher?

options.text: A, because drama makes the story memorable and the scale of the event is plainly impressive
A, because it was bigger in scale
B, because the assessor can see what B did and what changed
They score equally because both are valid

questions.hint: Clarity of personal evidence beats drama.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to use the same story for every Behaviour?

options.text: It breaks the word limit for the statement because the same context has to be repeated
It is not allowed in applications
It looks thin and may suggest there is little depth behind it
It makes the story less recent

questions.hint: Variety shows breadth.

questions.prompt: When can reusing a story for two Behaviours be acceptable?

options.text: When the word limit is very small and there is no room to describe another example
When the piece of work was large and the actions evidenced are genuinely different
When the second Behaviour is not the lead Behaviour
When the assessor will not compare the answers

questions.hint: Different actions from one large piece of work.

questions.prompt: What is the usual preference on recency?

options.text: Examples from the start of your career, since they show the longest record of experience
Examples from any time, at the candidate's choice
Only examples from your current post
Examples from the last two or three years unless the advert allows otherwise

questions.hint: Recent evidence is usually preferred.

questions.prompt: A good decision story is used for Developing Self and Others. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Higher marks because the story is strong and shows evidence of good judgement
Lower marks than a modest example that fits the Behaviour
Equal marks because assessors score the story in general
Disqualification from the sift

questions.hint: Fit matters more than impressiveness.

questions.prompt: What does independence mean as a test?

options.text: You worked without any other colleagues involved or any manager checking your decisions
You worked out what to do rather than being told
You had no manager involved
You made the decision at the end

questions.hint: It shows ownership.

questions.prompt: How can a story about a mistake still count as strong evidence?

options.text: It cannot, since assessors score only successes and treat any mistake as a weakness
Only when the mistake was made by someone else
By showing what you did to put it right and what you learned
Only for Developing Self and Others

questions.hint: Honest learning is valued.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before choosing an example?

options.text: The number of words the example would take and whether it fits in the word limit
The advert's wording of the Behaviour at the grade level and its scope
Whether the example involved the manager
Whether other applicants might use similar stories

questions.hint: Match scope to level.

questions.prompt: Which verb pattern makes an assessor's job easy?

options.text: Verbs from the Behaviour itself, such as decided, improved or led, with detail of what each involved
Verbs of effort and commitment such as tried, worked and persevered, repeated throughout the answer
Passive verbs that avoid naming the actor
Verbs describing what others did

questions.hint: Show the Behaviour in action.
